idiom_name: in-band type tag + tag-to-deserializer registry (identify, then parse)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: put a discriminator in the payload — an envelope field such as type or kind, or type identity the format introduces itself (writer schema, type URL, class descriptor, self-described tag) — and keep an explicit registry from tag to deserializer. Decode in two steps: read the tag from the envelope or peek at the first field, resolve it in the allow-list registry, then parse the body with the resolved deserializer; never let the tag select a type that is not registered, because a payload-directed constructor is an attacker-controlled entry point. The classic structure — a base type plus one subclass per message with a shared factory — is still justified when the decoded values must also be treated polymorphically in business logic.
code_sketch:
registry = {tag: decoder for tag, decoder in registered}   # allow-list, never a class name
kind = peek_tag(payload)                                    # step 1: identify only
decoder = registry.get(kind)
if decoder is None:
    dead_letter(payload, reason="unknown type")             # fail closed
value = decoder(payload.body)                               # step 2: parse with the resolved schema
pitfalls: Letting the tag name an unrestricted type instead of an allow-listed entry is the standard insecure-deserialization vulnerability.
Registering by language-level name makes refactoring a format break, and a missing registration fails only at runtime under a rare tag.
Repeating the tag per message and per nested element costs bandwidth; hoist it for homogeneous blocks or use a format that carries the schema once.
Untagged or structurally-inferred deserialization (trying each variant in order) is order-dependent, silently picks the wrong shape when variants overlap, and is slower than tag-directed dispatch.
Using class-relative names (short class name, minimal class name) as wire tags still breaks when two classes in different packages share the same short name.

Wrong move: treating a type_url or schema reference as a locator and fetching it from the network at decode time -> failure: a hostile tag makes the decoder contact an attacker-chosen URL (protobuf explicitly warns against contacting type URLs) -> instead: resolve tags only from a pre-populated local registry and treat the URL as an opaque identifier.

Wrong move: relying on magic-byte or schema-ID prefixes without validating the rest of the frame -> failure: a payload with a valid prefix and a garbage body reaches the decoder and surfaces as a confusing schema-mismatch error far from the corruption -> instead: treat the tag as identity only, then validate the decoded value against the resolved schema before use.

Wrong move: reusing one tag vocabulary across tenants or environments with independent registries -> failure: the same tag resolves to different types per reader, so a payload means different things downstream -> instead: publish the tag vocabulary as one owned contract and scope registries per tenant or topic.
